scenarios.scenarioText: Nexus Infrastructure Ltd. is a listed public company with a paid-up capital of ₹15 crores incorporated 9 years ago. On January 5, 2026, Buildmart Supplies Ltd., a trade creditor, served a written demand on Nexus for payment of ₹85,000 being dues for construction materials supplied. Nexus acknowledged receipt of the demand but made no payment and raised no dispute. By February 3, 2026, the amount remained entirely unpaid. Separately, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs received credible intelligence that Nexus's promoter-directors had been conducting the company's business with intent to defraud unsecured creditors by routing project funds through related-party shell entities. Nexus had also failed to file its annual returns and financial statements for financial years 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24 — three consecutive years. The creditor, the RoC, and a group of minority shareholders are each independently considering filing winding-up petitions before the NCLT.

questions.question: Buildmart Supplies Ltd. wants to file a winding-up petition before the NCLT under Section 271(a) of the Companies Act, 2013, on the ground that Nexus Infrastructure Ltd. is unable to pay its debts. Based strictly on the facts of this case, which statement is CORRECT?

options.A: The petition is maintainable — the demand of ₹85,000 remained unpaid for 29 days, which exceeds the 21-day statutory period under Section 271(a)
options.B: The petition is NOT maintainable — the demand amount of ₹85,000 is below the minimum threshold of a sum exceeding ₹1 lakh required under Section 271(a) for establishing inability to pay debts
options.C: The petition is NOT maintainable — Buildmart must first obtain a decree from a civil court before it can petition for winding up on inability to pay debts
options.D: The petition is maintainable — any creditor whose written demand remains unpaid for more than 21 days may establish inability to pay irrespective of the amount of the demand

questions.explanation: Section 271(a) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that a company shall be deemed unable to pay its debts if a creditor to whom the company owes a sum exceeding ₹1 lakh has served a written demand and the company has neglected to pay the sum for 21 days. Buildmart's claim is ₹85,000 — which is below ₹1 lakh. Therefore, this ground is NOT satisfied regardless of how many days have elapsed since the demand. The critical trap here is confusing this ₹1 lakh Companies Act threshold with the ₹1 crore minimum default threshold under the IBC — both are entirely distinct. Option A is wrong because the number of days is irrelevant if the amount threshold is not met. Option D is wrong as the minimum amount is an essential requirement, not merely the duration.

questions.question: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs received information that Nexus Infrastructure Ltd.'s business is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors through fund diversion. Under Section 271 of the Companies Act, 2013, which specific clause covers this as a ground for compulsory winding up by the Tribunal?

options.A: Section 271(b) — the company has passed a special resolution requesting that it be wound up by the Tribunal
options.B: Section 271(c) — the company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India
options.C: Section 271(d) — the affairs of the company have been conducted in a fraudulent or unlawful manner, or the persons in its management have been guilty of fraud or misconduct
options.D: Section 271(f) — the Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up

questions.explanation: Section 271(d) specifically covers situations where the affairs of the company have been conducted in a fraudulent or unlawful manner, or where the company was formed for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or where the persons concerned in its formation or management have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance, or misconduct. The diversion of project funds through shell entities to defraud creditors falls squarely within this ground. Section 271(f) (just and equitable) is a residual ground used when no specific ground fits — where a specific ground like (d) applies, that is the precise provision to invoke. Options (b) and (c) are clearly inapplicable to these facts.

questions.question: Nexus Infrastructure Ltd. has failed to file its annual returns and financial statements for three consecutive financial years (2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24). Does this non-filing constitute a valid ground for compulsory winding up under Section 271(e) of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Yes — three consecutive years of non-filing is sufficient; the Act requires only three years of default to establish this ground
options.B: No — Section 271(e) requires default in filing for FIVE consecutive financial years; three consecutive years of default does not satisfy the statutory threshold
options.C: Yes — any two or more years of non-filing constitutes a ground for compulsory winding up under Section 271(e)
options.D: No — non-filing of annual returns is not a ground for winding up; it merely attracts monetary penalties under Section 92

questions.explanation: Section 271(e) provides that a company may be wound up by the Tribunal if it has made a default in filing its financial statements or annual returns with the Registrar for five consecutive financial years. Nexus has defaulted for only three consecutive years — which falls short of the five-year statutory threshold. This is a precision-tested numerical trap: the threshold is specifically FIVE, not three or two. Option A incorrectly states three years is sufficient. Option C (any two years) is entirely without basis. Option D is wrong as Section 271(e) does establish non-filing as a winding-up ground — but only when the five-year threshold is met.

questions.question: Based on the facts established — specifically that Nexus Infrastructure Ltd.'s affairs have been conducted fraudulently under Section 271(d) — can the Registrar of Companies (RoC) file a winding-up petition on this ground under Section 272 of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Yes — the RoC is an eligible petitioner for all six grounds listed under Section 271 without any restriction
options.B: Yes — the RoC can petition on fraud grounds under Section 271(d) but must first obtain prior written sanction from the Central Government
options.C: No — a proviso to Section 272(1) expressly bars the RoC from presenting a winding-up petition on the grounds specified in clauses (b) and (d) of Section 271(1)
options.D: No — only the Central Government (and not the RoC) has standing to petition for winding up on grounds of fraudulent conduct under Section 271(d)

questions.explanation: Section 272(1) lists the persons competent to petition for compulsory winding up: the company, contributories, RoC, a person authorised by the Central Government, and in a Sec 271(f) case, the Central or State Government. However, the proviso to Section 272(1) expressly states that the Registrar shall NOT be entitled to present a petition for winding up on the grounds specified in clauses (b) and (d) of Section 271(1). Since the fraud ground falls under clause (d), the RoC is statutorily barred from petitioning on this ground. Option A is wrong — there are explicit restrictions. Option B invents a 'prior sanction' requirement that does not exist. Option D is overbroad — the Central Government can authorise another person; it need not itself petition.

questions.question: Nexus Infrastructure Ltd. itself decides to present a winding-up petition before the NCLT. Under Section 272(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, which document is MANDATORY for the company to file along with its own winding-up petition?

options.A: A special resolution passed at a general meeting of shareholders, irrespective of the ground on which the petition is filed
options.B: A security deposit of ₹25,000 with the NCLT as a precondition for the petition being heard
options.C: A Statement of Affairs of the company, disclosing its assets, liabilities, creditors, and debtors
options.D: A certificate from the statutory auditor confirming the company is unable to continue as a going concern

questions.explanation: Section 272(5) specifically mandates that where a company presents a petition for its own winding up, it shall, along with the petition, file a Statement of Affairs of the company in the prescribed form. This statement discloses the company's financial position including assets, liabilities, names of creditors, outstanding debts, and details of debtors — enabling the NCLT and Official Liquidator to understand the company's affairs from the outset. Option A is wrong — a special resolution is the ground for winding up under Sec 271(b) but is not a mandatory accompaniment when a company petitions on other grounds. Option B (₹25,000 deposit) is the security deposit under Section 214 for investigation applications — not winding-up petitions. Option D (auditor's certificate) is not prescribed under Section 272.

scenarios.scenarioText: Meridian Exports Pvt. Ltd. is a solvent private company with a paid-up capital of ₹2 crores. After successfully completing its business purpose, the shareholders unanimously agreed to close down operations. The company has a Board of 6 directors. On February 10, 2026, a Board meeting was held at which 4 directors (a majority) made a Declaration of Solvency. The declaration stated that the directors had made a full inquiry into the company's affairs and were of the opinion that the company would be able to pay all its debts in full within 3.5 years from the commencement of winding up. The declaration was accompanied by a statement of assets and liabilities as at February 8, 2026. It was filed with the RoC for registration on February 12, 2026. The shareholders subsequently held a general meeting on March 25, 2026 — 43 days after the declaration — at which they passed a special resolution to wind up the company voluntarily. At the same meeting, they also appointed a liquidator.

questions.question: The Declaration of Solvency made by the directors of Meridian Exports Pvt. Ltd. states that the company can pay all its debts within 3.5 years from the commencement of winding up. Is this Declaration of Solvency valid for the purposes of a Members' Voluntary Winding Up under Section 305(1) of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Yes — 3.5 years is a commercially reasonable estimate and Section 305 permits any reasonable time period
options.B: No — Section 305(1) requires that the declaration state that all debts will be paid within a period NOT exceeding 3 years from commencement of winding up; 3.5 years exceeds the statutory maximum
options.C: Yes — provided all creditors have been individually notified and no objection has been raised within 30 days
options.D: No — only independent directors may make the Declaration of Solvency; executive directors are excluded from making such a declaration

questions.explanation: Section 305(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires that the Declaration of Solvency contain a statement that the directors have made a full inquiry into the company's affairs and are of the opinion that the company shall be able to pay its debts in full within a period NOT EXCEEDING THREE YEARS from the commencement of winding up. A declaration stating '3.5 years' exceeds the statutory ceiling and is therefore legally invalid. The consequence of an invalid declaration is significant — the voluntary winding up cannot proceed as a Members' Voluntary Winding Up and instead defaults to a Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up. Option A (any reasonable period) and Option C (creditor notification) have no basis in Section 305. Option D (only independent directors) is a fictitious restriction.

questions.question: Assuming the Declaration of Solvency had validly stated that all debts would be paid within 2 years, and it was filed with the RoC on February 12, 2026, the shareholders passed the special resolution to wind up on March 25, 2026 — which is 43 days after the declaration was made. Under Section 305(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, is the timing of the special resolution compliant?

options.A: Yes — there is no prescribed time limit between the Declaration of Solvency and the shareholders' special resolution for winding up
options.B: Yes — a special resolution passed within 45 days of the declaration is compliant under Section 305(2)
options.C: No — the special resolution must be passed within five weeks (35 days) immediately following the declaration; 43 days exceeds this limit, making the declaration of no effect
options.D: No — the special resolution must be passed within 30 days of the declaration; 43 days is non-compliant

questions.explanation: Section 305(2)(a) provides that the Declaration of Solvency shall have no effect for the purposes of voluntary winding up unless it is made within the FIVE WEEKS immediately preceding the date of the passing of the resolution for winding up, and is delivered to the Registrar for registration before that date. Five weeks = 35 days. The general meeting resolution was passed on March 25, which is 43 days after the declaration made on February 10 — exceeding the 5-week window by 8 days. As a result, the declaration has no legal effect, and the winding up would proceed as a Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up instead. Option B (45 days) and Option D (30 days) both state incorrect time limits. Option A (no time limit) directly contradicts the statutory requirement.

questions.question: Assume the Declaration of Solvency for Meridian Exports Pvt. Ltd. was validly made and the Members' Voluntary Winding Up commenced. Within 18 months, it becomes clear that the company's debts CANNOT be fully paid within the 2-year period stated in the declaration — a major debtor has become insolvent, wiping out ₹80 lakhs of expected recoveries. Under Section 305(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, what legal PRESUMPTION arises against the 4 directors who signed the declaration?

options.A: No presumption arises — the directors are protected because unforeseen events (debtor insolvency) occurred after the declaration was made
options.B: It shall be presumed, until the contrary is shown, that the directors who made the declaration had REASONABLE grounds for the opinion expressed — the burden is on creditors to disprove this
options.C: It shall be presumed, until the contrary is shown, that the directors who made the declaration did NOT have reasonable grounds for the opinion expressed — the burden shifts to the directors to prove they had reasonable basis
options.D: The presumption arises only if the debts remain unpaid for more than 5 years; since the declared period was 2 years, no presumption applies

questions.explanation: Section 305(3) provides that if the company is wound up in pursuance of a resolution passed within five weeks of the declaration, and its debts are NOT paid or provided for in full within the period stated in the declaration, it shall be PRESUMED until the contrary is shown that the director(s) who made the declaration DID NOT HAVE REASONABLE GROUNDS for the opinion expressed in it. This is a REVERSE burden — the directors must affirmatively prove they had reasonable grounds. The fact that the debtor's insolvency was 'unforeseen' is a defence the directors could raise, but the burden is on THEM to prove it. Option A incorrectly absolves directors automatically. Option B reverses the statutory presumption (says reasonable grounds are presumed — the opposite of the law). Option D invents a 5-year trigger that does not exist. The scenario's specific fact (₹80 lakh debtor insolvency) is what triggers this provision.

questions.question: The Declaration of Solvency for Meridian Exports Pvt. Ltd. was accompanied by a statement of assets and liabilities dated February 8, 2026 — two days before the declaration on February 10. Had the directors instead attached a statement dated December 28, 2025 — a full 44 days before the declaration — arguing it was the date of the last completed monthly closing, would the Declaration of Solvency satisfy the requirement of Section 305(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Yes — there is no prescribed maximum gap; any statement of assets and liabilities prepared within the same financial year is acceptable
options.B: Yes — the Act merely requires a statement of assets and liabilities, with no requirement regarding how recent the date must be
options.C: No — Section 305(2)(b) requires the statement to be as at the 'latest practicable date' before the making of the declaration; a 44-day-old statement is unlikely to satisfy this standard when a more recent statement could practicably have been prepared
options.D: No — the statement must be dated on the exact same date as the declaration itself, failing which the declaration is void

questions.explanation: Section 305(2)(b) requires the declaration to contain a statement of assets and liabilities as at the 'LATEST PRACTICABLE DATE' before the making of the declaration. This is not a fixed-number rule but a PRACTICAL STANDARD — the statement must be as current as it is practically possible to prepare. In the actual Meridian scenario, February 8 (2 days before February 10) clearly satisfies this test. But a statement dated December 28 — 44 days prior — raises a serious question: was a more recent statement practicably available? If the company's books were current and a monthly closing was completed in January 2026, then a December 2025 statement is NOT the 'latest practicable date' and the declaration would have no legal effect. Option A invents a 'same financial year' standard that does not exist. Option B ignores the 'latest practicable date' requirement entirely. Option D is overly rigid — the Act does not require the same date, only the latest practicable date.

questions.question: Assume the Members' Voluntary Winding Up of Meridian Exports Pvt. Ltd. is validly commenced. Partway through the winding-up process, the appointed company liquidator forms the opinion that the company will NOT be able to pay its debts in full within the 2-year period stated in the Declaration of Solvency. What is the liquidator's statutory obligation under Section 308 of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: The liquidator may independently extend the repayment period by filing a revised Declaration of Solvency on behalf of the directors
options.B: The liquidator must immediately file an application before the NCLT to convert the winding up into a compulsory Tribunal winding up
options.C: The liquidator must forthwith summon a meeting of the creditors and lay before them a statement of the assets and liabilities of the company; thereafter, the winding up continues as a Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up
options.D: The liquidator must resign and notify the shareholders, who will appoint a new liquidator to reassess the position

questions.explanation: Section 308 of the Companies Act, 2013 deals with the conversion of a Members' Voluntary Winding Up to a Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up. If the liquidator forms the opinion at any time during a Members' VWU that the company will not be able to pay its debts in full within the period stated in the Declaration of Solvency, the liquidator shall forthwith summon a meeting of creditors and lay before the meeting a statement in the prescribed form of the assets and liabilities of the company. Thereafter, the provisions as to Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up apply as if the company had passed a creditors' winding-up resolution at the time of summoning the meeting. The liquidator does NOT go to the NCLT (Option B) — the conversion is self-executing. The liquidator does NOT file a revised declaration (Option A) or resign (Option D).

scenarios.scenarioText: Vega Hospitality Ltd. is a private company with a paid-up capital of ₹5 crores that operated a chain of boutique hotels. Following a prolonged economic downturn, the company's directors assessed that the company's total liabilities of ₹7.2 crores significantly exceeded its total realisable assets of ₹3.1 crores. The directors concluded they could not honestly make a Declaration of Solvency. On August 1, 2026, the company held a general meeting of its members at which a special resolution was passed for voluntary winding up. A creditors' meeting was held on August 2, 2026. At the creditors' meeting, the directors placed before the creditors a full statement of the company's affairs and a list of creditors with their estimated claims. The members' meeting had nominated Mr. Arjun Mehta as liquidator. At the creditors' meeting, creditors representing 65% in value nominated Ms. Priya Shah as liquidator. A director of the company disagreed and filed an application before the NCLT within 5 days of the creditors' nomination, seeking a Tribunal order that Mr. Arjun Mehta be appointed instead.

questions.question: Since Vega Hospitality Ltd.'s directors determined they could not make a Declaration of Solvency, what type of voluntary winding up is this, and under Section 306(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, when must the creditors' meeting be held?

options.A: Members' Voluntary Winding Up; a creditors' meeting must be held within 14 days of the members' general meeting
options.B: Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up; the creditors' meeting must be held on the same day as the members' resolution OR on the next day following that day
options.C: Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up; the creditors' meeting must be held within 7 days of the date of the special resolution
options.D: Members' Voluntary Winding Up; a creditors' meeting is discretionary and is held only when the liquidator specifically requires it

questions.explanation: Since the directors are unable to make a Declaration of Solvency (because liabilities exceed assets), this is a Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up (CVW) — not a Members' VWU. Section 306(1) requires that in a CVW, the company shall cause a meeting of its creditors to be held on the day on which the resolution for voluntary winding up is passed OR on the next day following that day. The members' resolution was passed on August 1, 2026, and the creditors' meeting was held on August 2 — the very next day. This is compliant. Options A and C state incorrect timelines (14 days and 7 days). Option D misclassifies the type and incorrectly calls the creditors' meeting discretionary.

questions.question: At the creditors' meeting of Vega Hospitality Ltd. held on August 2, 2026, the directors presented the Statement of Affairs showing total liabilities of ₹7.2 crores and total realisable assets of ₹3.1 crores. A bank creditor (owed ₹2.8 crores) alleged that the directors had undervalued the company's immovable properties by at least ₹1 crore and that the Statement of Affairs was materially misleading. Under the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following CORRECTLY describes the directors' legal exposure if the Statement of Affairs presented at the creditors' meeting is later proven to contain materially false statements?

options.A: The directors face no personal liability — the Statement of Affairs is a good-faith estimate and directors are protected from liability for valuation judgments
options.B: Only the company (as a legal entity) can be held liable for inaccurate disclosures; individual directors are insulated during winding up
options.C: A director who makes any statement in the Statement of Affairs which is materially false, knowing it to be false or not believing it to be true, shall be punishable with imprisonment and fine under the penalty provisions of the Act
options.D: The creditors can set aside the entire winding-up resolution if they prove the Statement of Affairs was inaccurate, requiring the company to restart its business operations

questions.explanation: Under the Companies Act, 2013, directors bear personal responsibility for the accuracy of the Statement of Affairs presented to creditors. Section 306(2) requires directors to lay the statement before the creditors' meeting. If a director makes any statement that is materially false, knowing it to be false or without believing it to be true, the director shall be liable to punishment under the penalty provisions. In this scenario, the bank creditor alleges a ₹1 crore undervaluation of immovable properties — if proven, this is a material misstatement that could expose the directors personally. Option A incorrectly shields directors from accountability. Option B attempts to use corporate veil during winding up which does not apply to personal liability for false statements. Option D wrongly suggests the winding-up resolution itself can be reversed — the remedy is personal liability of the directors, not undoing the winding up.

questions.question: At the creditors' meeting of Vega Hospitality Ltd., the creditors nominated Ms. Priya Shah as liquidator. The members had already nominated Mr. Arjun Mehta at the earlier meeting. Under Section 310 of the Companies Act, 2013, which person is the liquidator by default, and what remedy does the law provide for the other side?

options.A: Mr. Arjun Mehta (nominated by members) is the liquidator since the members' meeting preceded the creditors' meeting in time; creditors have no override power in a voluntary winding up
options.B: Ms. Priya Shah (nominated by creditors) is the liquidator by default; however, any director, member, or creditor may apply to the NCLT within 7 days of the creditors' nomination for an order directing that Mr. Mehta be appointed instead or jointly
options.C: Both nominees must be appointed as joint liquidators to represent the interests of both members and creditors
options.D: Neither nominee is automatically appointed; the conflict must be resolved by the RoC appointing a third-party liquidator

questions.explanation: Section 310 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that in a Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up, where the creditors and the company nominate different persons as liquidator, the person nominated by the CREDITORS shall be the liquidator. The creditors have economic priority in a CVW since the company is insolvent. Therefore, Ms. Priya Shah is the default liquidator. However, a proviso to Section 310 grants relief: any director, member, or creditor may, WITHIN SEVEN DAYS of the creditors' nomination, apply to the Tribunal for an order that the company's nominee be appointed instead or jointly, or that some other person be appointed. In this scenario, the director filed an application within 5 days — within the 7-day window — making it a valid application. Option A (members' nominee prevails) is the exact opposite of the legal rule. Options C and D are not the statutory defaults.

questions.question: The director of Vega Hospitality Ltd. filed an application before the NCLT within 5 days of the creditors' nomination seeking Mr. Arjun Mehta's appointment. Under Section 310, which of the following orders can the NCLT pass on hearing this application?

options.A: The NCLT can only confirm the creditors' nominee (Ms. Priya Shah) — it has no power to replace or add to her appointment once creditors have validly nominated
options.B: The NCLT may direct that Mr. Arjun Mehta (company's nominee) be appointed as liquidator INSTEAD OF Ms. Priya Shah, or JOINTLY WITH her, or appoint a completely different third person
options.C: The NCLT must dismiss the application since the director filed it without the prior written consent of at least 10% of the members
options.D: The NCLT can only appoint both nominees jointly — it has no power to replace the creditors' nominee outright

questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 310 gives the Tribunal three specific options when hearing such an application: (i) direct that the company's nominee be liquidator INSTEAD OF the creditors' nominee; (ii) direct that both be appointed JOINTLY; or (iii) appoint some OTHER person as liquidator instead of the creditors' nominee. The Tribunal has full discretion among these three options based on the merits. Option A (NCLT cannot interfere) directly contradicts the proviso. Option C invents a '10% member consent' requirement that has no basis in Section 310. Option D limits the NCLT to only joint appointments, which is incorrect — the Tribunal can also replace the creditors' nominee entirely.

questions.question: In the Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up of Vega Hospitality Ltd., the liquidator needs to distribute the company's ₹3.1 crore realised assets. Which of the following is NOT an option available to a secured creditor (owed ₹2 crores, holding security over assets worth ₹1.5 crores) in a voluntary winding up under the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Realise the security independently outside the winding-up pool and prove for the ₹0.5 crore shortfall as an unsecured creditor
options.B: Surrender the security to the liquidator and prove for the full ₹2 crore debt as an unsecured creditor alongside other unsecured creditors
options.C: Value the security at ₹1.5 crores, retain possession of it, and prove for the ₹0.5 crore balance as an unsecured creditor
options.D: Apply unilaterally to the NCLT to stay the voluntary winding up and convert it to a compulsory Tribunal winding up solely because it is a secured creditor with unsatisfied claims

questions.explanation: Secured creditors in a voluntary winding up under the Companies Act have three recognised options: (i) realise security independently and claim shortfall (Option A); (ii) surrender security and prove for full debt as unsecured (Option B); or (iii) value security, retain it, and prove for the balance (Option C). All three are valid. Option D — applying unilaterally to convert voluntary winding up to compulsory winding up merely on the basis of being an unsatisfied secured creditor — is NOT a recognised power. To seek compulsory winding up, a creditor would need to establish an independent ground under Section 271 and be a competent petitioner under Section 272. Being a secured creditor with outstanding dues does not by itself entitle a party to override a valid voluntary winding-up process.

scenarios.scenarioText: Pinnacle Textiles Ltd. is a listed public company with a paid-up capital of ₹20 crores. A group of minority shareholders filed a petition before the NCLT under Section 272 seeking compulsory winding up, primarily on the grounds that it was 'just and equitable' due to a complete breakdown of mutual trust among shareholders. Pinnacle had also failed to file its annual returns and financial statements for all five financial years from 2020-21 to 2024-25. After a hearing at which Pinnacle contested both grounds, the NCLT found that the breakdown of trust was genuine, satisfying the just and equitable ground under Section 271(f). The NCLT made a winding-up order. It then appointed the Official Liquidator attached to the Tribunal to conduct the winding up. After realising all assets and settling all claims, the Official Liquidator completed the winding-up process. The company also had outstanding dues in the Statement of Affairs that it had not previously disclosed — these were discovered only after the winding-up order was passed.

questions.question: The NCLT observed that Pinnacle Textiles Ltd. had not filed its annual returns or financial statements for five consecutive financial years (2020-21 to 2024-25). Which ground under Section 271 is independently established by this fact alone?

options.A: Section 271(a) — inability to pay debts, inferred from persistent non-compliance with statutory obligations
options.B: Section 271(d) — affairs conducted in a fraudulent or unlawful manner, since non-filing is an unlawful act
options.C: Section 271(e) — default in filing financial statements or annual returns with the Registrar for five consecutive financial years
options.D: Section 271(f) — just and equitable, since continued non-filing makes it inequitable for the company to continue

questions.explanation: Section 271(e) is the specific provision that covers this precise situation: a company which has made a default in filing its financial statements or annual returns with the Registrar for FIVE CONSECUTIVE FINANCIAL YEARS is liable to be wound up compulsorily by the Tribunal. Pinnacle has defaulted for exactly five consecutive years — satisfying this threshold precisely. Section 271(a) (inability to pay) requires a specific monetary demand and period; non-filing does not imply inability to pay. Section 271(d) (fraudulent conduct) requires affirmative evidence of fraudulent intent — mere non-filing does not constitute fraud. Section 271(f) is a residual ground; where Section 271(e) specifically covers the situation, (e) is the applicable provision.

questions.question: After hearing the petition, the NCLT found the 'just and equitable' ground established. Under Section 274 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following is NOT among the powers available to the NCLT when it hears a winding-up petition?

options.A: Dismiss the petition with or without costs
options.B: Adjourn the hearing of the petition conditionally or unconditionally
options.C: Make any interim order it considers fit
options.D: Order the minority shareholders who filed the petition to pay damages to Pinnacle Textiles Ltd. for loss of future business opportunities caused by the filing of the petition

questions.explanation: Section 274 of the Companies Act, 2013 specifies the Tribunal's powers on hearing a winding-up petition. The Tribunal may: (a) dismiss the petition with or without costs; (b) adjourn the hearing conditionally or unconditionally; (c) make any interim order it thinks fit; or (d) make a winding-up order. Ordering petitioners to pay 'damages for loss of future business opportunities' has absolutely no basis under Section 274. The Tribunal may award costs against an unsuccessful petitioner — but awarding damages for business loss is a civil remedy entirely outside the scope of Section 274. This question tests whether students confuse the Tribunal's power to award costs (which exists) with compensation for business loss (which does not).

questions.question: After the NCLT passed the winding-up order for Pinnacle Textiles Ltd., the Official Liquidator discovered that the company had undisclosed outstanding dues — a secured bank loan of ₹4 crores not reflected in the originally filed accounts. The bank now wants to file a recovery suit against Pinnacle in the District Court. Under Section 279 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the legal position regarding suits against a company after a winding-up order has been made?

options.A: All existing and future legal proceedings against the company are permanently extinguished and cannot be pursued in any forum once the winding-up order is passed
options.B: No suit or other legal proceeding shall be commenced or continued against the company except by LEAVE OF THE TRIBUNAL and subject to such terms as the Tribunal may impose
options.C: Secured creditors like the bank are exempt from any restriction and can freely commence or continue suits without requiring Tribunal permission
options.D: Legal proceedings are automatically transferred from all courts to the SFIO for consolidated investigation and adjudication

questions.explanation: Section 279 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that when a winding-up order has been made, no suit or other legal proceeding shall be commenced or, if already pending, shall be proceeded with against the company EXCEPT BY LEAVE OF THE TRIBUNAL and subject to such terms as the Tribunal may impose. This creates a statutory moratorium (analogous to but distinct from the IBC Section 14 moratorium) that prevents a disorderly scramble by creditors. In this scenario, the bank — despite being a secured creditor owed ₹4 crores — must obtain Tribunal leave before filing a recovery suit. The bank's secured status gives it NO exemption from this requirement. Option A is too drastic — proceedings are stayed pending leave, not permanently extinguished. Option C wrongly exempts secured creditors. Option D invents an SFIO transfer that has no statutory basis under Section 279.

questions.question: After the winding-up order was passed for Pinnacle Textiles Ltd., the Official Liquidator required the directors and promoters to submit a Statement of Affairs. The directors submitted the statement exactly 30 days after the winding-up order, but it was incomplete — the undisclosed ₹4 crore bank loan was omitted. The Official Liquidator rejected it and demanded a corrected version citing special reasons. The directors submitted the corrected Statement of Affairs 12 days later — a total of 42 days from the date of the winding-up order. Under Section 281 of the Companies Act, 2013, is the corrected submission within the permissible time limit?

options.A: No — the maximum permissible period is 30 days from the winding-up order with no extension available; 42 days is entirely outside the statutory timeline
options.B: Yes — the Official Liquidator may extend the initial 30-day period by a further period not exceeding 15 days for special reasons; 42 days (30 + 12) falls within the maximum permissible 45-day window
options.C: No — the Official Liquidator can only grant a further extension of 7 days (total 37 days); 42 days exceeds the maximum of 37 days
options.D: Yes — the Official Liquidator may grant unlimited extensions at his discretion; there is no statutory cap on the total time for submission

questions.explanation: Section 281(1) provides that the Statement of Affairs must be submitted within 30 DAYS from the date of the winding-up order. The Official Liquidator may, for SPECIAL REASONS, extend this period by a further period NOT EXCEEDING 15 DAYS. Total maximum permissible = 30 + 15 = 45 days. The corrected statement at 42 days (30 + 12 additional) is within this 45-day window, and the undisclosed ₹4 crore bank loan constitutes a 'special reason' justifying the extension. The student must: (1) know the 30-day initial period, (2) know the 15-day extension exists, (3) compute that 42 < 45, and (4) recognise that the incomplete statement with omitted liabilities constitutes special reasons. Option A (no extension available) is incorrect — extension exists. Option C invents a 7-day cap. Option D (unlimited extensions) overstates the OL's discretion — the cap is strictly 15 days.

questions.question: After all assets of Pinnacle Textiles Ltd. have been completely realised and all claims settled by the Official Liquidator, what is the precise procedural sequence under Section 302 of the Companies Act, 2013 for the company to be formally dissolved?

options.A: The company is automatically dissolved three months after the Official Liquidator files the final accounts with the RoC, without any further Tribunal order
options.B: The Official Liquidator makes a report to the Tribunal upon complete winding up; the Tribunal then makes a dissolution order; the Official Liquidator sends a certified copy to the RoC within 30 days
options.C: The shareholders of the company must pass a resolution confirming dissolution at an extraordinary general meeting before the Tribunal can make a dissolution order
options.D: The Official Liquidator applies directly to the Central Government for a gazette notification declaring the dissolution, bypassing the Tribunal at the final stage

questions.explanation: Section 302(1) provides that when the affairs of a company have been completely wound up, the Official Liquidator shall make a report to the Tribunal and apply to the Tribunal for an order for dissolution. The Tribunal shall thereupon make an order that the company be dissolved from the date of such order. Section 302(2) further requires that the Official Liquidator shall, within THIRTY DAYS of the dissolution order, send a certified copy of the order to the RoC, who shall make an entry accordingly in the Register. The company ceases to exist from the date of the NCLT's dissolution order. Dissolution is NOT automatic (Options A, D). Shareholders have absolutely no role in this process (Option C) — the entire point of compulsory winding up is that the Tribunal, not the shareholders, controls the dissolution.

scenarios.scenarioText: Aurora Chemicals Ltd. is a public company with a paid-up capital of ₹12 crores. The company has three outstanding claims against it: (i) Techno Supplies Ltd., a trade creditor, is owed ₹95,000, unpaid for 30 days despite a written demand; (ii) National Finance Bank, a financial creditor under IBC, is owed ₹2.5 crores; and (iii) RawMat Pvt. Ltd., a raw materials supplier, is owed ₹75 lakhs as an operational creditor under IBC. The company's Board has passed a resolution at a Board meeting resolving to wind up the company, but no general meeting of shareholders has been held and no special resolution has been passed by shareholders. Additionally, a group of minority shareholders believes that the promoter family, which holds 71% of the shares, has repeatedly denied dividends to the public shareholders for 8 consecutive years without any commercial or business reason — despite the company being consistently profitable. The minority shareholders are simultaneously exploring winding up under Section 271(f) and an oppression petition under Section 241.

questions.question: Techno Supplies Ltd. (owed ₹95,000) and RawMat Pvt. Ltd. (owed ₹75 lakhs) both want to initiate proceedings against Aurora Chemicals Ltd. Which of the following correctly states the eligibility of BOTH parties to initiate insolvency/winding-up proceedings?

options.A: Techno Supplies can file a winding-up petition under Companies Act Section 271(a); RawMat can file an IBC application under Section 9 — both proceedings can run simultaneously
options.B: Techno Supplies CANNOT file under Section 271(a) as ₹95,000 is below the ₹1 lakh threshold; RawMat CAN file under IBC Section 9 as ₹75 lakhs exceeds the ₹1 crore threshold
options.C: Techno Supplies CANNOT file under Section 271(a) as ₹95,000 is below the ₹1 lakh threshold; RawMat CANNOT file under IBC Section 9 as ₹75 lakhs is below the ₹1 crore minimum default threshold
options.D: Both are barred from filing since National Finance Bank, as the senior financial creditor, has the exclusive right to initiate proceedings first

questions.explanation: Two entirely separate thresholds apply — one for each law. (i) Companies Act, Section 271(a): to establish inability to pay debts, the creditor's written demand must be for a sum EXCEEDING ₹1 lakh, unpaid for 21 days. Techno Supplies' claim of ₹95,000 is below ₹1 lakh — it CANNOT use this ground. (ii) IBC Section 4: the minimum default threshold to trigger the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) is ₹1 crore. RawMat's ₹75 lakh claim is below ₹1 crore — it CANNOT file under IBC either. Both are blocked by their respective thresholds. Option A incorrectly allows both. Option B incorrectly allows RawMat under IBC (₹75L < ₹1 crore). Option D invents a seniority-based exclusivity that does not exist in law.

questions.question: Aurora Chemicals Ltd.'s Board has passed a board resolution to wind up the company, but no general meeting has been held and no special resolution has been passed by shareholders. Under Section 271(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, does this board resolution constitute a valid ground for compulsory winding up by the Tribunal?

options.A: Yes — a board resolution unanimously passed by the directors represents the company's collective decision and satisfies Section 271(b)
options.B: No — Section 271(b) requires a SPECIAL RESOLUTION passed at a GENERAL MEETING of members; a board resolution is legally insufficient to establish this ground
options.C: Yes — since the Board holds delegated authority from shareholders, a board resolution is equivalent to a special resolution for the purposes of voluntary actions like winding up
options.D: No — only the Central Government can resolve for winding up under Section 271(b); a private company resolution has no effect

questions.explanation: Section 271(b) provides that a company may be wound up by the Tribunal if the company has passed a 'special resolution' requiring it to be wound up by the Tribunal. A 'special resolution' under the Companies Act means a resolution passed at a general meeting of members with the votes cast in its favour not less than three times the votes cast against it. A board resolution is an entirely different instrument — it represents the decision of the Board of Directors, not the members as a body. The Board cannot substitute for shareholders on matters that the Act reserves for a general meeting. Option A (board = company decision) and Option C (delegation equivalence) mischaracterise the distinct legal roles of the Board and the general meeting. Option D incorrectly restricts Section 271(b) to the Central Government.

questions.question: The minority shareholders of Aurora Chemicals Ltd. want to file a winding-up petition under Section 271(f) (just and equitable) based on 8 years of unjustified dividend denial by the 71% majority. Before ordering winding up on the just and equitable ground, which of the following considerations must the NCLT take into account?

options.A: The NCLT has no power to consider alternative remedies — once the just and equitable ground is established, a winding-up order is mandatory
options.B: The NCLT should first consider whether an alternative remedy is available to the petitioners (such as an order under Section 242 for oppression/mismanagement) and whether winding up is the only just and equitable outcome, since winding up is a remedy of last resort
options.C: The NCLT must dismiss the winding-up petition since the shareholders should first exhaust their remedy of filing a complaint before the SEBI for investor protection
options.D: The NCLT must wind up the company immediately if the just and equitable ground is technically established, since delay would further prejudice the minority shareholders

questions.explanation: The 'just and equitable' ground under Section 271(f) is a residual, discretionary ground. Established case law (including the House of Lords decision in Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries and subsequent Indian jurisprudence) holds that winding up on this ground is a remedy of LAST RESORT. Before ordering dissolution, the NCLT must consider whether the petitioners have an adequate alternative remedy — most relevantly, whether relief could be granted under Section 242 (Tribunal's power to regulate company affairs, order buyback, change management, etc.) or under Section 241 (oppression/mismanagement). The Supreme Court of India has held that if the petitioner can obtain adequate relief without winding up the company, that alternative should be preferred. Option A removes judicial discretion entirely. Option C imposes an irrelevant pre-requisite of SEBI complaint. Option D mandates immediate winding up on mere technical establishment — which contradicts the discretionary nature of Section 271(f).

questions.question: National Finance Bank (owed ₹2.5 crores) wants to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against Aurora Chemicals Ltd. under IBC Section 7. Aurora's lawyer argues that since the Board has already resolved to wind up voluntarily, IBC proceedings are not maintainable. Which statement is CORRECT?

options.A: The lawyer is correct — once the Board has resolved for voluntary winding up, any creditor's insolvency application under IBC becomes non-maintainable
options.B: The lawyer is incorrect — a mere board resolution to wind up has no legal effect on the company's status; IBC proceedings are fully maintainable since the default of ₹2.5 crores exceeds the ₹1 crore threshold
options.C: The IBC proceedings are maintainable but must be automatically stayed once the shareholders pass a special resolution for voluntary winding up at a general meeting
options.D: National Finance Bank must first file a petition under Companies Act Section 271 and obtain a winding-up order before it can separately apply under IBC

questions.explanation: A board resolution to wind up the company has NO legal effect under the Companies Act — it is not a 'special resolution' (which requires a general meeting), and no voluntary winding-up has legally commenced. The company continues to exist as a going concern in every legal sense. Even if a valid general meeting special resolution were passed, this would not automatically bar a creditor from filing under IBC — the IBC operates on its own framework independent of the Companies Act. National Finance Bank's default of ₹2.5 crores far exceeds the ₹1 crore minimum IBC threshold under Section 4 read with Section 7 — making the CIRP application fully maintainable. Options A and C incorrectly extend the effect of a board resolution. Option D invents a pre-requisite of Companies Act proceedings before IBC, which has no basis in law.
questions.section: IBC Section 7 read with Section 4; Companies Act Section 271

questions.question: In the event Aurora Chemicals Ltd. is eventually wound up voluntarily and a company liquidator is appointed, the liquidator needs to sell the company's immovable factory property. Under Section 309 of the Companies Act, 2013, can the liquidator sell the factory by private contract WITHOUT obtaining sanction from the Tribunal or the committee of inspection?

options.A: No — all sales of immovable property must be approved by the NCLT irrespective of the mode of sale
options.B: Yes — Section 309(1) allows the company liquidator to sell the movable and immovable property of the company by public auction OR by private contract without requiring any Tribunal sanction
options.C: No — private contract sales of immovable property always require NCLT sanction; only public auction sales can be conducted freely
options.D: Yes — but only if the sale value does not exceed ₹1 crore; beyond that, NCLT sanction is mandatory

questions.explanation: Section 309(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 lists the powers that the company liquidator may exercise WITHOUT the sanction of the Tribunal or committee of inspection. These include: (c) selling the movable AND immovable property and actionable claims of the company by PUBLIC AUCTION or by PRIVATE CONTRACT, with power to transfer the whole thereof to any person or company, or to sell the same in parcels. The liquidator therefore has broad authority to sell assets — including immovable property — by whichever mode (auction or private contract) best serves the winding-up estate, without needing NCLT approval for each sale. Powers that DO require sanction (Sec 309(2)) include: paying a class of creditors in full, compromising debts, or accepting shares as consideration for a sale. Options A, C, and D all impose restrictions that Section 309(1) does not.

scenarios.scenarioText: Zenith Pharma Ltd. is a public company with a paid-up capital of ₹25 crores, incorporated 14 years ago, engaged in manufacturing generic pharmaceuticals. In November 2025, a creditor (Medicore Chemicals Ltd., owed ₹3.5 crores) served a statutory written demand, which Zenith neglected to pay for 28 days. The NCLT admitted a winding-up petition filed by Medicore under Section 271(a) and passed a winding-up order on January 15, 2026. On the same date, the NCLT appointed Mr. Raghav Desai, an Insolvency Professional registered with IBBI, as the Company Liquidator. Over the next few months, creditors raised concerns about Mr. Desai's handling of the estate — specifically, that he had delayed realisation of perishable pharmaceutical inventory and had appointed his brother-in-law's firm as the estate valuer without competitive bidding. The NCLT took suo motu cognizance and initiated proceedings regarding the liquidator. Meanwhile, Zenith's promoter-directors argued that since the company had two operating subsidiaries (one in Gujarat and one in Tamil Nadu), the winding-up order should not have been published widely, as it would damage the subsidiaries' business reputation and banking relationships.

questions.question: Under Section 270 of the Companies Act, 2013, winding up of a company may be carried out in two specific modes. Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies both modes?

options.A: Compulsory winding up by the Tribunal, and Voluntary winding up (which itself may be Members' Voluntary or Creditors' Voluntary)
options.B: Compulsory winding up by the Tribunal, and Summary winding up by the Registrar of Companies for small companies
options.C: Voluntary winding up by shareholders, and Administrative dissolution by the Central Government without Tribunal intervention
options.D: Compulsory winding up by the High Court, and Voluntary winding up supervised by the Company Law Board (CLB)

questions.explanation: Section 270 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that the winding up of a company may be either (a) by the Tribunal (compulsory winding up), or (b) voluntary. The voluntary mode is further subdivided into Members' Voluntary Winding Up (where a Declaration of Solvency is made) and Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up (where no such declaration can be made). Option B invents a 'summary winding up by RoC' that does not exist under the 2013 Act. Option C fabricates an 'administrative dissolution by CG' route. Option D references the High Court and CLB — the CLB was replaced by the NCLT under the 2013 Act, and winding-up jurisdiction now lies with the NCLT, not the High Court.

questions.question: When Medicore Chemicals Ltd. filed the winding-up petition against Zenith Pharma Ltd. before the NCLT, which of the following procedural requirements under Section 273 of the Companies Act, 2013 must be complied with BEFORE the petition is heard?

options.A: The petitioner must serve a copy of the petition on the company and the company must be given a reasonable opportunity to make representations to the Tribunal before the hearing date
options.B: No notice to the company is required — the Tribunal can pass a winding-up order ex parte without hearing the company
options.C: The petitioner must obtain prior written approval from the Central Government before the NCLT can entertain any winding-up petition
options.D: The petitioner must deposit 50% of the claimed debt with the NCLT as security before the petition is listed for hearing

questions.explanation: Section 273 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that where a petition for winding up is filed before the Tribunal, a copy of the petition shall be served on the company and the company shall be given a reasonable opportunity of making its representations before the Tribunal before the petition is heard. This ensures principles of natural justice are followed. The NCLT cannot pass a winding-up order without notice to the company (Option B is wrong). No Central Government approval is needed for filing a petition (Option C is fabricated). There is no requirement to deposit 50% of the debt (Option D is a fictitious requirement). The scenario establishes that Zenith had the opportunity to be heard since the order was passed after a proper hearing.

questions.question: The NCLT appointed Mr. Raghav Desai, an Insolvency Professional registered with IBBI, as the Company Liquidator for Zenith Pharma Ltd. Under Section 275 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following statements about the appointment of the Company Liquidator is INCORRECT?

options.A: The Tribunal may appoint an Official Liquidator or an Insolvency Professional as the Company Liquidator at the time of passing the winding-up order
options.B: The Insolvency Professional so appointed must be registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI)
options.C: The Company Liquidator appointed by the Tribunal has no obligation to submit a report on the affairs of the company within any fixed time frame — the timeline is entirely at the liquidator's discretion
options.D: The Tribunal may replace the Company Liquidator if sufficient cause is shown

questions.explanation: Section 275 provides that the Tribunal shall appoint an Official Liquidator or an Insolvency Professional (registered with IBBI) as the Company Liquidator. Options A and B correctly state this. Option D is also correct — the Tribunal retains power to replace the liquidator (Section 276). However, Option C is INCORRECT because the Company Liquidator is required under Section 281 to submit a preliminary report and under Section 291 to submit a first report to the Tribunal. These are not discretionary timelines. The liquidator must report on the company's affairs within prescribed timeframes. The scenario highlights Mr. Desai's delayed handling of inventory — which is precisely the kind of conduct that invites Tribunal scrutiny of whether the liquidator is fulfilling time-bound obligations.

questions.question: Creditors raised concerns about Mr. Raghav Desai appointing his brother-in-law's firm as estate valuer without competitive bidding, and the NCLT took suo motu cognizance. Under Section 276 of the Companies Act, 2013, on what grounds can the Tribunal remove a Company Liquidator?

options.A: The Tribunal can remove the Company Liquidator only if the liquidator is convicted of a criminal offence — administrative misconduct or conflict of interest is insufficient
options.B: The Tribunal may, on due cause shown, remove the Company Liquidator and appoint another in his place; 'due cause' encompasses misconduct, conflict of interest, incompetence, or failure to perform duties faithfully
options.C: Only the creditors' committee can remove the Company Liquidator by passing a resolution with 75% majority; the Tribunal has no independent removal power
options.D: The Company Liquidator can only be removed by the Central Government on the recommendation of the IBBI, not by the Tribunal

questions.explanation: Section 276 provides that the Tribunal may, on due cause shown, remove the Company Liquidator and appoint another liquidator in his place. The term 'due cause' is deliberately broad and encompasses any conduct that renders the liquidator unfit or unsuitable to continue — including conflict of interest (appointing a relative's firm as valuer), incompetence (delaying realisation of perishable inventory), and failure to perform duties with requisite care. In the Zenith scenario, Mr. Desai's appointment of his brother-in-law's firm without competitive bidding creates a clear conflict of interest constituting 'due cause.' Option A sets an impossibly high bar (criminal conviction) that the Act does not require. Option C gives removal power to creditors' committee, not the statute. Option D invents a CG/IBBI removal mechanism.

questions.question: The promoter-directors of Zenith Pharma Ltd. argued that the winding-up order should not be published widely to protect the subsidiaries' reputation. Under Section 277 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the mandatory requirement regarding notification of a winding-up order?

options.A: The winding-up order is a confidential Tribunal order and is communicated only to the company, the petitioner, and the RoC — no public notification is required
options.B: The Tribunal shall, within a period not exceeding 15 days from the date of the order, cause intimation of the order to be sent to the Official Liquidator and the RoC, and the order must be published in the Official Gazette and in a leading English and vernacular newspaper circulating in the district of the registered office
options.C: Publication is mandatory only if the company's paid-up capital exceeds ₹50 crores; below this threshold, notification to the RoC alone is sufficient
options.D: The promoter-directors may obtain a stay on publication from the NCLT if they demonstrate potential reputational harm to related group companies

questions.explanation: Section 277 mandates that when a winding-up order is made, the Tribunal shall, within a period not exceeding 15 days from the date of the passing of the order, cause intimation thereof to be sent to the Official Liquidator and to the Registrar. The order shall also be published in the Official Gazette and in a leading English newspaper and a leading vernacular newspaper circulating in the district where the registered office of the company is situated. This publication is MANDATORY and cannot be suppressed to protect reputational interests of subsidiaries or group companies. The promoter-directors' argument has no legal basis — public notification serves the vital purpose of alerting all creditors, stakeholders, and third parties. Option A (confidential) contradicts the mandatory publication requirement. Option C invents a capital threshold. Option D fabricates a stay mechanism that does not exist under Section 277.

scenarios.scenarioText: Horizon Realty Ltd. is a public company with a paid-up capital of ₹18 crores, engaged in commercial real estate development. The company's major project — a 40-storey commercial tower in Mumbai — stalled after the principal contractor abandoned the project mid-construction. On March 1, 2026, the NCLT passed a winding-up order against Horizon Realty on the 'just and equitable' ground. Three weeks BEFORE the winding-up order (on February 8, 2026), the Managing Director had sold the company's prime Pune land parcel (valued at ₹6 crores) to his wife's family trust for ₹1.2 crores — a transaction made without Board approval. Separately, on February 20, 2026, a secured creditor (Apex Bank, owed ₹12 crores) had obtained an attachment order from the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) against Horizon's Hyderabad office. Additionally, a trade creditor (Buildright Contractors, owed ₹45 lakhs) had filed a recovery suit in the Bombay High Court, which was pending when the winding-up order was passed. After the winding-up order, Horizon continued to exist in name — the Company Liquidator took charge. The liquidator discovered that the MD had made several suspicious payments totalling ₹90 lakhs to shell companies in the 4 months before the winding-up order, which appeared to be preferential transfers designed to benefit certain related-party creditors over others.

questions.question: After the NCLT passed the winding-up order against Horizon Realty Ltd. on March 1, 2026, the company's promoters argued that the company has ceased to exist as a legal entity and therefore cannot be subjected to further proceedings. Under Section 278 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the CORRECT legal position regarding the company's status after a winding-up order?

options.A: The company is immediately dissolved and ceases to exist from the date of the winding-up order; all further proceedings must be against the directors personally
options.B: The company continues to exist as a body corporate with all its powers until it is dissolved by a specific dissolution order of the Tribunal under Section 302, but the Board's powers are displaced by the Company Liquidator
options.C: The company is suspended for a maximum period of 2 years during which the liquidator operates; if winding up is not completed within 2 years, the company is revived automatically
options.D: The company's legal identity merges with the Official Liquidator's office; the company and the OL become the same legal entity for all purposes

questions.explanation: Section 278 provides that an order for winding up a company shall operate in favour of all the creditors and all the contributories of the company as if it had been made on the joint petition of a creditor and a contributory. Crucially, the company does NOT cease to exist upon the winding-up order — it continues as a body corporate until the Tribunal makes a specific dissolution order under Section 302. The corporate identity persists; only the management shifts from the Board to the Company Liquidator. This distinction is vital because the company can still be party to legal proceedings, own property, and have obligations during the winding-up period. Option A confuses winding-up order with dissolution order — a common student error. Option C invents an automatic revival mechanism. Option D fabricates a legal identity merger.

questions.question: Buildright Contractors had a pending recovery suit for ₹45 lakhs in the Bombay High Court when the winding-up order was passed on March 1, 2026. Under Section 280 of the Companies Act, 2013, what happens to this pending suit?

options.A: The suit continues in the Bombay High Court without any change — pending suits are not affected by a winding-up order
options.B: The suit is automatically dismissed with liberty to Buildright to file a fresh claim with the Company Liquidator
options.C: The suit or proceeding pending in any court against the company shall be transferred to the Tribunal, and the Tribunal shall dispose of it on the merits
options.D: The suit is stayed permanently and Buildright can only file a proof of debt with the Company Liquidator; it can never resume the suit

questions.explanation: Section 280 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that where any suit or other legal proceeding is pending in any court by or against the company at the date of the winding-up order, the court in which such suit or proceeding is pending shall, on the application of the Tribunal, transfer such suit or proceeding to the Tribunal, and the Tribunal may dispose of the same. This centralises all litigation involving the company before the Tribunal conducting the winding up. Buildright's Bombay High Court suit would be transferred to the NCLT. Option A ignores the mandatory transfer requirement. Option B wrongly says the suit is 'dismissed.' Option D confuses Section 280 (transfer) with Section 279 (stay requiring leave) — the suit is not permanently stayed but transferred for disposal on merits.

questions.question: The Managing Director of Horizon Realty Ltd. sold the company's Pune land parcel (valued ₹6 crores) to his wife's family trust for ₹1.2 crores on February 8, 2026 — three weeks before the winding-up order of March 1, 2026. This transfer was without Board approval. Under Section 283 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the legal status of this transfer?

options.A: The transfer is valid — any transaction completed before the winding-up order cannot be challenged, as the winding-up order operates only prospectively
options.B: The transfer is void unless the Tribunal otherwise orders, because it is a voluntary transfer of property made AFTER the commencement of winding up; the commencement date relates back to the date of presentation of the petition, not the date of the winding-up order
options.C: The transfer can be set aside only if Buildright Contractors (as an unsecured creditor) specifically files a separate civil suit challenging it in the High Court
options.D: The transfer is voidable only if the land was the company's SOLE remaining asset; if the company has other assets, the transfer stands

questions.explanation: Section 283 provides that any transfer of property, movable or immovable, or any delivery of goods made by or against a company after the commencement of the winding up shall, unless the Tribunal otherwise orders, be VOID. Critically, the 'commencement of winding up' in a compulsory winding up relates back to the date of presentation of the winding-up petition — NOT the date of the winding-up order. This means the February 8 transfer, though made before the March 1 order, is likely void if the petition was presented before February 8. Even if the petition was filed after February 8, the transfer at ₹1.2 crores for a ₹6 crore asset to a related party (MD's wife's family trust) without Board approval is a textbook case where the Tribunal would NOT exercise its discretion to validate the transfer. Option A wrongly assumes prospective-only operation. Option C invents a separate civil suit requirement. Option D creates a 'sole asset' condition that does not exist.

questions.question: Apex Bank had obtained an attachment order from the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) against Horizon Realty Ltd.'s Hyderabad office on February 20, 2026 — nine days before the winding-up order of March 1, 2026. Under Section 284 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the effect of the winding-up order on this DRT attachment?

options.A: The DRT attachment order takes priority over the winding-up order because it was obtained first in time, following the principle 'first in time, first in right'
options.B: Where any company is being wound up by the Tribunal, any attachment, distress, or execution put in force against the estate or effects of the company AFTER the commencement of winding up shall be void
options.C: The attachment order remains valid but Apex Bank must pay 10% of the attached property's value to the liquidator as a winding-up fee
options.D: The DRT attachment is suspended for 180 days; if winding up is not completed within 180 days, the attachment automatically revives

questions.explanation: Section 284 provides that where any company is being wound up by the Tribunal, any attachment, distress, or execution put in force, without leave of the Tribunal, against the estate or effects of the company AFTER the commencement of the winding up shall be VOID. As with Section 283, 'commencement' relates back to the date of petition presentation, not the order date. If the petition was presented before February 20, the DRT attachment is void. This provision ensures that no individual creditor gains an unfair advantage over others during the winding-up process — the principle of pari passu (equal treatment) governs. Option A incorrectly applies a common law priority principle that is expressly overridden by statute. Option C invents a fee mechanism. Option D fabricates a 180-day suspension period.

questions.question: The Company Liquidator discovered that the MD of Horizon Realty Ltd. had made payments totalling ₹90 lakhs to shell companies in the 4 months before the winding-up order, which appeared to be preferential transfers favouring related-party creditors. Under Section 289 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following CORRECTLY describes the law on preferential payments in winding up?

options.A: Preferential payments are voidable only if made within 30 days immediately preceding the commencement of winding up; payments made 4 months prior are outside the look-back period
options.B: Any transfer of property or payment made within 1 year before the commencement of winding up in favour of any creditor is a fraudulent preference and is automatically void without any further inquiry
options.C: A transfer by way of giving a creditor a preference over other creditors, made within 6 months before the commencement of winding up (or 2 years in case of a related party), shall be deemed a fraudulent preference and shall be invalid — but only if the company was unable to pay its debts at the time of the transfer
options.D: Preferential payment provisions apply only to unsecured creditors; payments to related-party entities are outside the scope of Section 289

questions.explanation: Section 289 deals with fraudulent preference in winding up. A transfer of property, movable or immovable, delivery of goods, payment, execution, or other act relating to property made or done by or against a company within a period of 6 MONTHS before the commencement of winding up (or 2 YEARS in the case of a related party) which has the effect of giving such creditor a preference over the other creditors shall be deemed a fraudulent preference and shall be invalid. However, this applies only where the company was unable to pay its debts at the time of the transaction. The ₹90 lakh payment to shell companies (related parties) falls within the 2-year look-back period. The key conditions are: (1) made within the statutory period, (2) preferential effect, and (3) company's inability to pay debts at the time. Option A (30 days) is far too short. Option B omits the inability-to-pay condition and uses 1 year. Option D wrongly excludes related parties.

scenarios.scenarioText: Cosmos Steel Ltd. is a public company with a paid-up capital of ₹30 crores that was incorporated 20 years ago. The NCLT ordered its compulsory winding up on September 15, 2025 under Section 271(a) on the petition of a major creditor. The Company Liquidator commenced the task of identifying all persons liable to contribute to the assets of the company. Cosmos had 4,500 current members. Additionally, Mr. Vikram Joshi, who had transferred his 50,000 shares (fully paid up) to his nephew 8 months before the commencement of winding up, contended he had no further liability. The company also had 2,000 preference shareholders whose preference shares were due for redemption 2 years ago but had not been redeemed. The Company Liquidator calculated that the company's realisable assets fell short of its liabilities by ₹8 crores, requiring calls on contributories. Two former directors — Mr. Ashok Nair and Ms. Ritu Bhatia — were found to have misapplied ₹3.5 crores of company funds by sanctioning interest-free loans to their personal associates without Board approval, during the 3 years preceding the winding-up order. The Company Liquidator filed an application before the NCLT seeking to recover this amount from the directors personally.

questions.question: Under Section 285 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the Company Liquidator's obligation regarding the identification of contributories in the winding up of Cosmos Steel Ltd.?

options.A: The Company Liquidator must prepare a list of contributories within 60 days of the winding-up order and file it with the NCLT; the Tribunal then settles the list after hearing objections
options.B: The Company Liquidator shall, with all convenient speed after a winding-up order has been made, settle a list of contributories — the list distinguishes between persons who are contributories in their own right and persons who are contributories as representatives of or liable to the debts of others
options.C: Only the RoC can prepare the list of contributories based on the company's Register of Members; the Company Liquidator has no role in this process
options.D: The list of contributories is prepared by the statutory auditor, not the Company Liquidator, as it involves financial determination of liability

questions.explanation: Section 285 provides that the Tribunal shall, as soon as may be after making a winding-up order, cause the Company Liquidator to settle a list of contributories, and the Company Liquidator shall rectify the register of members in all cases where rectification is required, and every contributory shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be liable to contribute to the assets of the company the amount which he is liable to contribute. The list distinguishes between persons who are contributories in their own right and those who are contributories as representatives. Option A invents a specific 60-day timeline that is not prescribed — the standard is 'with all convenient speed.' Option C wrongly assigns this to the RoC. Option D incorrectly assigns it to the statutory auditor.

questions.question: Mr. Vikram Joshi transferred his 50,000 fully paid-up shares to his nephew 8 months before the commencement of winding up. He argues he has no liability as a contributory since he is no longer a member. Under Section 286 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following CORRECTLY states the liability of a past member as a contributory?

options.A: A past member is NOT liable as a contributory if the shares transferred were fully paid up — contributory liability arises only for partly paid shares
options.B: A past member is liable as a contributory in respect of debts and liabilities contracted BEFORE he ceased to be a member, subject to the condition that he ceased to be a member not more than ONE YEAR before the commencement of winding up, and that the existing members are unable to satisfy the contributions required of them
options.C: A past member who transferred shares within 2 years of winding up is treated identically to a current member — there is no distinction in liability
options.D: Past members have no liability whatsoever once a valid transfer has been registered in the company's records — the liability is entirely extinguished upon transfer

questions.explanation: Section 286 provides that a past member shall not be liable to contribute if he has ceased to be a member for one year or more before the commencement of the winding up. A past member is liable to contribute only in respect of the debts and liabilities of the company contracted before he ceased to be a member, and only if it appears that the existing contributories (current members) are unable to make the contributions required. Mr. Vikram Joshi transferred shares 8 months before commencement — within the 1-year look-back period — making him potentially liable as a past member contributory. However, the fact that his shares were fully paid up is critical: on fully paid shares, there is no further amount 'unpaid' to call. Option A is partially correct in practice but doesn't state the full legal position. Option B correctly identifies all three conditions. Option C wrongly extends to 2 years. Option D wrongly says liability is entirely extinguished.

questions.question: The Company Liquidator of Cosmos Steel Ltd. calculated an ₹8 crore shortfall between realisable assets and liabilities. Under Section 287 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal has the power to make calls on contributories to make up this shortfall. Which of the following statements about calls on contributories is CORRECT?

options.A: The Tribunal can make calls on contributories ONLY for the amount remaining unpaid on their shares; it cannot make calls exceeding the nominal value of the shares
options.B: The Tribunal may, at any time after making a winding-up order, make calls on all or any of the contributories to the extent of their liability, for payment of any money which the Tribunal considers necessary to satisfy the debts and liabilities of the company and the costs, charges, and expenses of winding up
options.C: Calls on contributories can only be made by the Company Liquidator independently without any Tribunal order; the Tribunal merely ratifies the calls after the fact
options.D: Calls on contributories are prohibited in a compulsory winding up — they are permitted only in voluntary winding up where the company's directors retain authority

questions.explanation: Section 287 empowers the Tribunal to make calls on all or any of the contributories of the company to the extent of their liability for payment of any money which the Tribunal considers necessary to satisfy the debts and liabilities of the company, and the costs, charges, and expenses of winding up, and for the adjustment of the rights of the contributories among themselves. The call is made by the TRIBUNAL, not by the liquidator independently (Option C is wrong). Option A is partially correct in that liability is limited to the amount unpaid on shares, but the section's scope is broader — it covers all liability under Section 285-286, not just unpaid share amounts. Option D wrongly restricts calls to voluntary winding up only.

questions.question: Cosmos Steel Ltd. has 2,000 preference shareholders whose preference shares were due for redemption 2 years ago but were never redeemed. In the winding up, these preference shareholders want to be treated as creditors (not members) for the unredeemed amount. Under Section 288 of the Companies Act, 2013, which principle governs the adjustment of rights among different classes of contributories?
