options.A: The Tribunal shall adjust the rights of the contributories among themselves, and distribute any surplus among the persons entitled thereto — preference shareholders rank AHEAD of equity shareholders in the return of capital
options.B: All contributories — equity and preference — are treated identically in a winding up with no preferential ranking; the principle of pari passu applies to all members equally
options.C: Preference shareholders with unredeemed shares are automatically converted to secured creditors and rank ahead of all unsecured creditors in the distribution waterfall
options.D: Only equity shareholders are contributories; preference shareholders are never included in the list of contributories regardless of the terms of their shares

questions.explanation: Section 288 provides that the Tribunal shall adjust the rights of the contributories among themselves and distribute any surplus among the persons entitled thereto. In a winding up, preference shareholders have preferential rights over equity shareholders for the return of capital — this is the fundamental nature of preference shares under Section 43 of the Companies Act. The 2,000 preference shareholders whose shares were due for redemption would rank ahead of equity shareholders for capital repayment. However, they are NOT creditors (Option C is wrong) — they remain members/contributories with a preferential ranking. Option B incorrectly applies pari passu among all member classes. Option D wrongly excludes preference shareholders from the contributory list.

questions.question: The Company Liquidator filed an application before the NCLT to recover ₹3.5 crores from Mr. Ashok Nair and Ms. Ritu Bhatia, the former directors who sanctioned interest-free loans to personal associates without Board approval. Under Section 303 of the Companies Act, 2013, what power does the Tribunal have in this situation?

options.A: The Tribunal can only recommend criminal prosecution to the Central Government; it has no power to assess monetary damages or order personal recovery against directors
options.B: The Tribunal may assess damages against any director or officer of the company who has misapplied, retained, or become liable or accountable for any money or property of the company, or been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust — and compel such person to repay or restore the money or property with interest
options.C: The Tribunal's power under Section 303 is limited to a maximum recovery of ₹1 crore per director, regardless of the actual amount misapplied
options.D: Only the Company Liquidator can file the application under Section 303; creditors and contributories have no standing to seek such an assessment

questions.explanation: Section 303 empowers the Tribunal to examine the conduct of any director, officer, or manager of the company and to assess damages against any such person who has misapplied or retained, or become liable or accountable for, any money or property of the company, or has been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. The Tribunal may compel such person to repay or restore the money or property (or any part thereof) with interest at such rate as the Tribunal thinks just. In this case, the ₹3.5 crore interest-free loans to personal associates without Board approval constitutes misapplication of company funds and breach of trust. Option A wrongly limits the Tribunal to criminal recommendation only. Option C invents a ₹1 crore cap. Option D is incorrect — while the liquidator typically files, the section also allows creditors and contributories to apply.

scenarios.scenarioText: Maple Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. is a private company (not an NBFC) with a paid-up capital of ₹4 crores that operated a fintech lending platform. After achieving its founders' exit plan, the Board of 5 directors decided to wind up voluntarily. On April 1, 2026, 3 directors (a majority of the total 5) held a Board meeting and made a Declaration of Solvency stating that the company could pay all its debts within 18 months. The declaration was verified by an affidavit sworn before a First Class Judicial Magistrate. It was delivered to the RoC on April 3, 2026. On April 28, 2026 — 27 days after the declaration — the members held a general meeting and passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up. At the same meeting, they appointed Mr. Sunil Kapoor as the company liquidator. Subsequently, Mr. Kapoor needed to compromise a disputed ₹40 lakh claim from a former vendor who threatened litigation. He also planned to accept shares of another company as part-consideration for selling Maple's software platform. Additionally, 4 months into the winding up, a secured creditor (owed ₹60 lakhs) approached Mr. Kapoor demanding full payment ahead of all other creditors, claiming the company's Declaration of Solvency guaranteed payment within 18 months.

questions.question: The Declaration of Solvency for Maple Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. was made by 3 out of 5 directors and was verified by an affidavit sworn before a First Class Judicial Magistrate. Under Section 304 of the Companies Act, 2013 (read with Section 305), which of the following statements about the formal requirements of the Declaration of Solvency is INCORRECT?

options.A: The declaration must be made by a majority of the directors at a Board meeting — 3 out of 5 satisfies this requirement
options.B: The declaration must be verified by an affidavit, and the affidavit may be sworn before a First Class Judicial Magistrate or a Notary
options.C: The declaration must be accompanied by a report of the company's auditors on the reasonableness of the directors' opinion regarding the company's ability to pay debts
options.D: The declaration must contain a statement of assets and liabilities as at the latest practicable date before the making of the declaration

questions.explanation: Under Section 304 and Section 305, the Declaration of Solvency must: (1) be made by a MAJORITY of directors at a Board meeting — 3/5 satisfies this (Option A is correct); (2) be verified by an AFFIDAVIT — it may be sworn before a First Class Judicial Magistrate (Option B is correct); (3) contain a statement of assets and liabilities as at the latest practicable date (Option D is correct per Section 305(2)(b)). However, Option C is INCORRECT — the Act requires the declaration to be accompanied by the AUDITOR'S REPORT on the profit and loss account of the company for the period from the last account date to the latest practicable date. This is not an auditor's report on the 'reasonableness of the directors' opinion' — the auditor certifies the financial statements, NOT the directors' solvency opinion. The directors themselves bear the responsibility for the opinion on solvency.

questions.question: The members of Maple Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up on April 28, 2026. Under Section 307 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the company's obligation regarding publication of this resolution?

options.A: No publication is required for a private company's voluntary winding-up resolution; publication is mandatory only for public companies
options.B: The company must give notice of the resolution by advertisement in the Official Gazette and also in a newspaper circulating in the district where the registered office is situated, within FOURTEEN DAYS of the passing of the resolution
options.C: The resolution must be published on the company's website within 7 days; no newspaper or gazette publication is needed
options.D: Publication is required only if the company has more than 200 members; Maple, being a private company with limited members, is exempt

questions.explanation: Section 307 provides that where a company has passed a resolution for voluntary winding up, the company shall, within FOURTEEN DAYS of the passing of the resolution, give notice of the resolution by advertisement in the Official Gazette and also in a newspaper circulating in the district where the registered office of the company is situated. This requirement applies to ALL companies — public or private — without any exemption based on company type, size, or number of members. The purpose is to notify all stakeholders, including unknown creditors, of the commencement of winding up. Option A wrongly exempts private companies. Option C invents a website-only requirement. Option D fabricates a member-count threshold.

questions.question: Mr. Sunil Kapoor, the company liquidator of Maple Financial Services Pvt. Ltd., wants to: (i) compromise the disputed ₹40 lakh vendor claim, and (ii) accept shares of another company as part-consideration for selling Maple's software platform. Under Section 309(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, which of these actions require the PRIOR SANCTION of the Tribunal?

options.A: Neither requires sanction — the company liquidator has unfettered discretion over all commercial decisions during winding up
options.B: Only the compromise requires sanction; accepting shares as consideration is within the liquidator's independent power under Section 309(1)
options.C: BOTH require prior sanction — Section 309(2) lists compromising claims exceeding a prescribed amount AND accepting shares or like interest as consideration among the powers exercisable ONLY with Tribunal sanction
options.D: Only accepting shares requires sanction; compromising claims is within the liquidator's power regardless of amount

questions.explanation: Section 309(2) lists specific powers that the Company Liquidator may exercise ONLY WITH THE SANCTION of the Tribunal. These include: (a) paying any class of creditors in full; (b) making any compromise or arrangement with creditors; and (c) compromising all calls, liabilities, and debts, and all claims whether present or future. Separately, Section 309(2) also requires sanction for accepting shares, policies, or other like interest as consideration for the sale of company property. Both of Mr. Kapoor's proposed actions — compromising the ₹40 lakh claim and accepting shares as consideration — fall squarely under Section 309(2) and require prior Tribunal sanction. This contrasts with Section 309(1) powers (like selling by auction or private contract, executing documents) which do NOT require sanction. Option A, B, and D each wrongly exclude one or both actions from the sanction requirement.

questions.question: The members' special resolution for voluntary winding up of Maple Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. was passed on April 28, 2026 — exactly 27 days after the Declaration of Solvency was made on April 1, 2026. The Declaration was delivered to the RoC on April 3, 2026. For the Members' Voluntary Winding Up to be validly constituted, which of the following conditions must ALL be satisfied simultaneously?

options.A: Declaration of Solvency by majority directors + filed with RoC + special resolution within 5 weeks + declaration states debts payable within 3 years — ALL four conditions must be met
options.B: Declaration of Solvency by any 2 directors + filed with RoC + special resolution within 45 days + declaration states debts payable within 5 years
options.C: Declaration of Solvency by unanimous Board + filed with RoC and NCLT + ordinary resolution within 30 days + declaration states debts payable within 2 years
options.D: Declaration of Solvency by majority directors + no filing requirement + special resolution at any time + declaration states debts payable within a 'reasonable period'

questions.explanation: For a valid Members' Voluntary Winding Up, ALL of the following must be simultaneously satisfied: (1) Declaration of Solvency made by a MAJORITY of directors at a Board meeting (Section 305(1)); (2) Declaration DELIVERED to the RoC for registration BEFORE the date of the special resolution (Section 305(2)(a)); (3) Special resolution passed WITHIN FIVE WEEKS (35 days) of the Declaration (Section 305(2)(a)); and (4) Declaration states debts will be paid within a period NOT EXCEEDING THREE YEARS (Section 305(1)). For Maple: 3/5 directors (majority ✓), filed April 3 before April 28 resolution (✓), 27 days < 35 days (✓), 18 months < 3 years (✓). All conditions are met. Option B: wrong on 2 directors, 45 days, 5 years. Option C: wrong on unanimity, NCLT filing, ordinary resolution, 2 years. Option D: wrong on no filing, no time limit, reasonable period.

questions.question: Four months into the Members' Voluntary Winding Up of Maple Financial Services Pvt. Ltd., the liquidator Mr. Sunil Kapoor has been paying creditors as their claims are verified. Under Section 300 of the Companies Act, 2013, what ongoing reporting obligation does the Company Liquidator have during a winding up that continues for more than one year?

options.A: No reporting obligation exists during the winding-up process; the liquidator files only a final report upon completion
options.B: The Company Liquidator must file an annual statement with the Tribunal and the Registrar showing the position of the liquidation, including a statement of accounts of receipts and payments and the position of the liquidation during the year
options.C: The liquidator must hold an annual general meeting of shareholders to present the winding-up progress report — identical to a normal company's AGM requirement
options.D: The Company Liquidator must file monthly reports with the IBBI detailing every transaction exceeding ₹1 lakh

questions.explanation: Section 300 provides that if the winding up of a company is not concluded within one year after its commencement, the Company Liquidator shall, within TWO MONTHS of the close of each subsequent financial year (or such other period as the Tribunal directs), file a statement in the prescribed form with the Tribunal and the Registrar, containing information on receipts, payments, and the position of the liquidation. This ensures ongoing transparency and accountability. Although Maple's winding up is only 4 months in, if it extends beyond one year, this obligation would kick in. Option A (no reporting until final) is incorrect — annual reporting is mandatory. Option C wrongly equates winding-up reporting with a normal AGM. Option D invents IBBI monthly reporting.

scenarios.scenarioText: Prism Logistics Ltd. is a public company with a paid-up capital of ₹10 crores that operated a nationwide freight and warehousing business. The company faced crippling losses after losing its three largest clients in rapid succession. A consortium of creditors (owed a collective ₹22 crores) filed a winding-up petition under Section 271(a), and the NCLT passed a winding-up order on June 1, 2026. The Company Liquidator, Ms. Anjali Menon (an Insolvency Professional), immediately took charge. She discovered that the company's books of account had not been properly maintained for the preceding 2 years — ledgers were incomplete, and several bank reconciliations were missing. She also found ₹15 lakhs lying in a bank account earmarked as 'unclaimed dividends' from FY 2022-23 that had never been transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF). The winding up progressed, but 10 months in, the Company Liquidator had not yet submitted her first report on the company's affairs to the Tribunal. A creditor (Speedway Transport, owed ₹1.8 crores) raised an objection before the Tribunal about this delay. Additionally, during the Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up of a DIFFERENT company (Trident Carriers Pvt. Ltd., a subsidiary of Prism), the liquidator of Trident needed to call a meeting of creditors to present the progress of the winding up. A dispute arose about whether the liquidator of Trident was obliged to convene such meetings and at whose request.

questions.question: Ms. Anjali Menon, the Company Liquidator of Prism Logistics Ltd., discovered that the company's books of account were improperly maintained for the preceding 2 years. Under Section 290 of the Companies Act, 2013, what specific obligation does the Company Liquidator have regarding the books of account during the winding-up process?

options.A: The Company Liquidator has no obligation regarding books — maintaining books is the directors' responsibility even during winding up
options.B: The Company Liquidator shall keep proper books in which he shall cause to be made entries or minutes of proceedings at meetings and of such other matters as may be prescribed; any contributory or creditor may, subject to the control of the Tribunal, inspect such books
options.C: The Company Liquidator must reconstruct the last 10 years of books before any distribution can be made to creditors
options.D: The books of account obligation transfers to the statutory auditor upon the passing of the winding-up order

questions.explanation: Section 290 imposes a clear obligation on the Company Liquidator to keep PROPER BOOKS in which entries or minutes of proceedings at meetings and such other matters as may be prescribed shall be made. Importantly, any contributory or creditor may, subject to the control of the Tribunal, inspect such books personally. This transparency mechanism ensures that the winding-up process is not opaque. In Ms. Menon's case, even though the company's pre-existing books were incomplete, she is independently obligated to maintain proper books from the commencement of her charge. Option A wrongly absolves the liquidator. Option C invents an impractical 10-year reconstruction requirement. Option D wrongly shifts the obligation to the statutory auditor.

questions.question: Ten months into the winding up of Prism Logistics Ltd., the Company Liquidator Ms. Anjali Menon has not yet submitted her first report to the Tribunal. Speedway Transport raised an objection about this delay. Under Section 291 of the Companies Act, 2013, within what time frame must the Company Liquidator submit the FIRST report to the Tribunal?

options.A: Within 30 days of the winding-up order — a preliminary statement of affairs only
options.B: Within 60 days from the date of the winding-up order, the Company Liquidator shall submit a preliminary report to the Tribunal containing information including the nature and estimated value of assets, amount and nature of liabilities, details of any fraud or misconduct discovered, and whether further inquiry is desirable
options.C: Within 6 months of the winding-up order — the first report is due only after substantial asset realisation has occurred
options.D: There is no fixed timeline; the Company Liquidator submits the report when she deems the investigation is sufficiently complete

questions.explanation: Section 291 requires the Company Liquidator to submit a PRELIMINARY REPORT to the Tribunal within SIXTY DAYS from the date of the winding-up order. This report must contain: (a) the nature and estimated value of the company's assets; (b) the amount and nature of the liabilities; (c) the causes of failure of the company; (d) whether in the liquidator's opinion further inquiry is desirable regarding any matter relating to the promotion, formation, or failure of the company; and (e) any other matters requiring the Tribunal's attention. Ms. Menon's failure to submit within 60 days — let alone 10 months — is a clear dereliction of this statutory duty and Speedway Transport's objection is well-founded. Option A (30 days) is incorrect. Option C (6 months) and Option D (no timeline) both understate the urgency.

questions.question: The Company Liquidator of Prism Logistics Ltd. found ₹15 lakhs in a bank account earmarked as 'unclaimed dividends' from FY 2022-23 that was never transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF). Under Section 301 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the Company Liquidator's obligation regarding money representing unclaimed dividends or undistributed assets that remain unclaimed during the winding up?

options.A: Unclaimed dividends belong to the company's general pool and can be distributed to known creditors without any special obligation
options.B: The Company Liquidator must pay such unclaimed or undistributed amount into the Company Liquidation Account in the scheduled bank; if the amount remains unclaimed for a prescribed period, it shall be transferred to the IEPF under Section 125
options.C: Unclaimed dividends are automatically forfeited to the Central Government upon the passing of the winding-up order
options.D: The Company Liquidator must return unclaimed dividends directly to the shareholders proportionately, bypassing the creditors entirely

questions.explanation: Section 301 provides that the Company Liquidator shall pay money representing unclaimed dividends or undistributed assets into a Company Liquidation Account in a scheduled bank. These amounts are held in trust for the persons entitled to them. If amounts remain unclaimed for the prescribed period, they are transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) under Section 125. The ₹15 lakhs of unclaimed dividends from FY 2022-23 must be deposited into the Company Liquidation Account and handled per this process — NOT merged into the general creditor pool (Option A), NOT forfeited to CG (Option C), and NOT distributed directly to shareholders bypassing creditors (Option D). The distinction between company assets and unclaimed dividends held in trust is critical.

questions.question: In the Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up of Trident Carriers Pvt. Ltd. (a subsidiary of Prism Logistics), a dispute arose about whether the liquidator must convene meetings of creditors during the progress of the winding up. Under Section 311 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following CORRECTLY states the liquidator's obligation regarding creditors' meetings in a Creditors' Voluntary Winding Up?

options.A: The liquidator has no obligation to convene any creditors' meeting after the initial meeting held under Section 306; creditors can only seek information through written correspondence
options.B: The liquidator may in his discretion convene meetings of creditors for the purpose of ascertaining their wishes — and shall also convene meetings on such occasions as the creditors by resolution or any one-tenth in value of the creditors may direct
options.C: Only the NCLT can direct the convening of creditors' meetings; the liquidator and creditors themselves have no power to initiate such meetings
options.D: Creditors' meetings can only be convened if the winding up has been ongoing for more than 2 years; shorter proceedings do not require interim meetings

questions.explanation: Section 311 provides that the liquidator shall summon meetings of the creditors or contributories as and when directed by the Tribunal or as and when the liquidator thinks fit for the purpose of ascertaining their wishes. Additionally, the liquidator shall convene meetings of creditors on such occasions as the creditors by resolution at any meeting, or ANY ONE-TENTH IN VALUE of the creditors, may direct. This dual mechanism — (i) liquidator's own discretion and (ii) creditor-directed meetings (requiring only 1/10 in value) — ensures transparency. The key trap is the 1/10 in value threshold for creditors to demand a meeting. Option A wrongly says no meetings after Section 306. Option C wrongly restricts the power to the NCLT only. Option D invents a 2-year minimum.

questions.question: Returning to the compulsory winding up of Prism Logistics Ltd. — the winding-up order was passed on June 1, 2026. A former employee of Prism who holds 500 shares wants to inspect the Company Liquidator's books to verify that employee dues are being properly accounted for. The Company Liquidator refuses inspection, stating that only creditors have inspection rights during winding up. Under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, is the Company Liquidator's refusal legally correct?

options.A: Yes — only creditors (not members or contributories) have the right to inspect the liquidator's books during compulsory winding up
options.B: No — under Section 290, any CONTRIBUTORY or CREDITOR may, subject to the control of the Tribunal, inspect the Company Liquidator's books; since the former employee is a shareholder (contributory), he has inspection rights
options.C: Yes — no person other than the Official Liquidator and the Tribunal has any right to inspect books during winding up; this is to protect commercially sensitive information
options.D: No — but only because the person is a former employee; members who are not employees have no inspection rights

questions.explanation: Section 290 expressly provides that any CONTRIBUTORY or CREDITOR may, subject to the control of the Tribunal, inspect the Company Liquidator's books. A 'contributory' includes every person liable to contribute to the assets of the company — which includes shareholders (current members). The former employee who holds 500 shares is a contributory by virtue of his shareholding, and therefore has the right to inspect the liquidator's books. The Company Liquidator's refusal is legally incorrect. The right is subject to the 'control of the Tribunal' — meaning the Tribunal may regulate the manner and timing of inspection, but cannot deny the right entirely. Option A incorrectly excludes contributories. Option C provides excessive secrecy that the Act does not mandate. Option D wrongly bases the right on employee status rather than contributory status.
